author: KarlOlofA
title: Workbench session loop
before:
Title: Workbench session loop
Kind: service
Links: agent-layer, app-state, mcp-connections, prompt-builder
Files:
  src/session.rs
  src/history.rs

Long-running coroutine that receives Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart) and owns the live agent.
With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the stored session id.
A generation counter drops events from killed processes.
Streamed events become chat items; file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done finishes the current graph job.
Every delivered message outside a job starts a chat turn in app-state, which Done settles against the baseline.
Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context.
When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state.
With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench sessions are remembered for the session history.

One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time.
With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id.
A generation counter drops events from killed processes.
Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline.
A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents in the same session with their tasks.
Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context.
When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state.
With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming.

author: KarlOlofA
title: Workbench session loop
before:
Title: Workbench session loop
Kind: service
Links: agent-layer, app-state, chat-sessions, mcp-connections, prompt-builder
Files:
  src/session.rs
  src/history.rs

One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume, Close; Close stops the agent and ends the loop) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time.
With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id.
A generation counter drops events from killed processes.
Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline.
A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents with their tasks: in the same session, or, when a block names a repository of the agent's project, in a new session in that repository.
A project-level agent gets the project's repositories as its context instead of the open folder's graph.
Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context.
When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state.
With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming.
Each agent runs on its own provider and model when it was started on one (AppState::agent_provider), otherwise on the ones in the settings; a spawn-agent block can name a provider and model for the new agent, and an unknown provider id is shown as an error instead of starting it.
The provider and model of a turn come from agent_provider.
A job's route wins over the agent's own provider.

Kind: service
Links: agent-layer, app-state, chat-sessions, mcp-connections, prompt-builder
Files:

One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume, Close; Close stops the agent and ends the loop) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time.
With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id.
A generation counter drops events from killed processes.
Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline.
A reply that ends with focus blocks has them stripped and shown as node choices in the chat, and a single match is focused on the graph right away.
Tool results of a scoped run are recorded as its live edits.
A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents with their tasks: in the same session, or, when a block names a repository of the agent's project, in a new session in that repository.
A project-level agent gets the project's repositories as its context instead of the open folder's graph.
Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context.
When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state.
With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming.
Each agent runs on its own provider and model when it was started on one (AppState::agent_provider), otherwise on the ones in the settings; a spawn-agent block can name a provider and model for the new agent, and an unknown provider id is shown as an error instead of starting it.
The provider and model of a turn come from agent_provider.
A job's route wins over the agent's own provider.

Title: Link routing
Kind: service
Links: graph-model
Files:
  src/routing.rs
Decisions:
  Links are routed orthogonally (right angles, rounded corners) with a shared trunk per target, modelled on Floorplan's ELK layered layout with ORTHOGONAL edge routing — because Floorplan's graphs are easier to read: no lines crossing everywhere, and links into the same node stack into the same path (instead of cubic Bezier curves straight from source to target) [chat 2026-11-20]
  A small router of our own in Rust instead of ELK — because There is no ELK for Rust, and our nodes keep user-pinned positions, so routes must work for any placement, not only a layout ELK computed (instead of embedding elkjs and letting it place and route) [chat 2026-11-20]
  Links cross each column through a gap between its nodes, jogging in the space between columns, and backward links do the same leftwards — because The project graph has real backward links (22 of 175 root links close a cycle, mostly into app-state, session-loop and chat-sessions), and long or backward links must never be drawn through nodes (instead of one horizontal detour above or below everything the link spans) [chat 2026-11-20]
  Links into different targets keep a lane apart in a gap when a free lane is near, and otherwise share the nearest lane — because A gap between rows only holds about two lanes; sharing reads better than a long loop round the whole column, and searching only the nearby gaps keeps routing fast (about 44 ms for 1500 nodes and 4000 links) (instead of always finding a free lane, which sent links round whole columns and took 200 ms on big graphs) [chat 2026-11-20]

Works out the path of every link on the graph canvas, Floorplan style: links leave a node's right side and enter the next node's left side, turning only at right angles with rounded corners.
Ports are spread down each side in the order of the other ends, and all links into one node share a vertical trunk just left of it, so they stack into one path.
A link passes every column between its ends through a gap between two nodes, stepping up or down in the space between columns, so no link is drawn through a node.
Backward links that close a cycle travel leftwards the same way.
